1:
Wesley reads the departure as a verdict on the riot — "so Demetrius gained nothing. Paul remained there till all was quiet" — while Henry has Paul take the disturbance as "an indication of Providence to him not to stay". Henry marks what the departure closes: after this, "to the end of the scripture-history of his life... we never find him breaking up fresh ground again, nor preaching the gospel where Christ had not been named". Chrysostom notes what the moment required: "there was need of much comforting after that uproar."

Calvin dwells on the cost of leaving. Paul "is enforced to leave his sons who were lately begotten, and had as yet scarce escaped shipwreck in the midst of the raging sea", the Ephesian church being "as yet slender and weak". Their consent he counts to their credit: "they were not wedded to themselves, but... careful for the kingdom of Christ."

What follows is famously compressed. Robertson observes that Luke "here condenses what was probably a whole year of Paul's life", and lists what is missing: the stay at Troas, the meeting with Titus in Macedonia, the visit to Illyricum, and the writing of the second letter to Corinth — "one of the most stirring experiences in Paul's whole career". His verdict on the silence is careful: "we do not have to say that Luke was ignorant of Paul's work during this period, only that he did not choose to enlarge upon it."

Ellicott fills the gap from the letters. Timothy and Erastus had been sent ahead about the discipline of the Corinthian church, and the coming of Stephanas cheered the apostle, who apparently wrote by them what is now the first epistle; he then "was led... to change his purpose, and to take the land journey through Macedonia instead of going by sea to Corinth". He adds a wider range still: Paul "had taken the great Roman road across Macedonia, and going westward to the shores of the Adriatic, had preached the gospel in Illyricum".

Which letters belong to these months is answered three ways. Barnes puts the second epistle to Corinth in Macedonia, sent by Titus, and Romans in Greece. Clarke agrees about Romans and says the three months were spent "partly... at Corinth, at Athens, and in Achaia", Paul having in Macedonia "suffered much, both from believers and infidels; but was greatly comforted by the arrival of Titus". Robertson goes furthest, holding that in this period Paul "may have written Galatians... and certainly did Romans".

The plot is reconstructed with increasing detail. Barnes infers that "the design of the Jews was to attack the ship in which he was about to sail, or to arrest him on ship-board". Clarke supplies a motive: they meant "to attack his ship on the voyage, seize his person, sell him for a slave, and take the money which he was carrying to the poor saints at Jerusalem". Ellicott sets it at Cenchreae, where "amid the stir and bustle of a port, they might do what they had failed to do before. Here there was no Gallio to curb their fury, and throw the ægis of his tolerant equity over their victim."

Robertson enters a distinction the others do not: "this plot is by the Jews, not the Judaizers whom Paul discusses so vehemently" in the later chapters of the second epistle — that trouble "seems now past" — but by "Paul's old enemies in Corinth". Calvin draws two morals from the change of route. It is an example of constancy, so that "all the servants of Christ" should "set this mirror before their eyes, that they may never faint through the wearisomeness of straits"; and a lesson in prudence, since by avoiding the ambush Paul "showeth that we must have regard of our life so far forth that we throw not ourselves headlong into the midst of dangers".
4:
Ellicott alone explains why a delegation was needed, and the reason is financial. Paul "was carrying up a large sum in trust for the churches of Judæa, and he sought to avoid even the suspicion of the malversations which the tongue of slanderers was so ready to impute to him. Representatives were accordingly chosen from the leading churches, who acting, as it were, as auditors of his accounts, would be witnesses that all was right." He infers from two of the names appearing in the Roman letter that "all of those here named were with St. Paul at Corinth".

The list itself is textually unsettled. Gill notes the first name appears as Sosipater in three of Beza's copies and as many of Stephens's, that the Ethiopic makes him "Peter, a citizen of Berea" and the Arabic "Sopater of Aleppo", while the Alexandrian, Beza's most ancient copy, the Complutensian and the Vulgate read "Sopater of Pyrrhus, the Berean; that is, the son of Pyrrhus". Chrysostom removes a different confusion: "how does he call Timothy a man of Thessalonica? This is not his meaning, but, Of Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus and Gaius: of Derbe, Timothy."

Whether the words into Asia belong there at all is a three-way disagreement. Robertson holds they do not: the Received Text adds them, "but the best documents... do not have it", and the phrase will not fit the facts, since "Trophimus went as far as Jerusalem and Aristarchus as far as Rome" — it "could apply only to Sopatros". Clarke reports the same evidence more modestly, the words being "wanting in two MSS., Erpen, the Ethiopic, Coptic, and Vulgate", and adds the difficulty: how men could accompany Paul into Asia and also "go before him, and tarry for him at Troas... is not so very clear". Wesley keeps the received reading and reads the itinerary out of it: "to Asia — there some of them left him. But Trophimus went with him to Jerusalem. Aristarchus, even to Rome."

Clarke offers Bishop Pearce's solution: not that they accompanied him but that "there followed him as far as to Asia; for they were not in his company till he set sail from Philippi". Robertson leaves the assembly point open — it is "not clear though probable that Luke means to say that these seven brethren, delegates of the various churches, started from Corinth with Paul" — allowing that "the party may really have been made up at Philippi".

Ellicott gives two reasons for sending them ahead. It let Paul "keep the Passover with the church at Philippi, starting after the days of unleavened bread", a feast "already assuming a new character as the festival of the Resurrection"; and "the disciples who went on in advance would announce St. Paul's coming to the church of Troas, and so there would be a full gathering to receive him".

The single word us is what both the moderns stop at. Barnes observes that it "shows that Luke had again joined Paul as his companion", last seen at Philippi in the house of Lydia, and admits that "why he remained there, or why he did not attend Paul in his journey to Athens, Corinth, Ephesus, etc., is not known". Robertson leaves the same question open — "Had Luke remained all this time in Philippi? We do not know" — but marks what follows: "he is with Paul now till Rome is reached."

Barnes explains the five days by weather, since Paul "when he crossed it on a former occasion, did it in two days; but the navigation of the sea is uncertain, and they were now probably hindered by contrary winds". Of the names he singles out Tychicus as "high in the confidence and affection of Paul", styled "a beloved brother, and faithful minister in the Lord" — while Trophimus would in the end be left at Miletum sick.
7:
The day is taken as evidence, and Calvin alone resists. Barnes says the verse shows "that this day was then observed by Christians as holy time", and thinks they "celebrated the Lord's Supper on every Lord's-day"; Clarke names it kyriake, which "among all Christians, afterwards took the place of the Jewish Sabbath"; Robertson notes that "for the first time here we have services mentioned on the first day of the week", though "liberty was allowed". Calvin thinks it may be a Sabbath after all — "either doth he mean the first day of the week... or else some certain Sabbath. Which latter thing may seem to me more probable" — before conceding the Hebrew idiom, and adding that "Paul waited for the Sabbath, that the day before his departure he might the more easily gather all the disciples into one place".

Ellicott takes the same evidence further, then qualifies it socially. The passage proves "that the Church had already begun to observe the weekly festival of the Resurrection in place of, or, where the disciples were Jews, in addition to, the weekly Sabbath"; but "those who were slaves, or freed-men still in service, under heathen masters could not transfer to it the rigid abstinence from labour which characterised the Jewish Sabbath" — which is why the meeting is in the evening.

Why the sermon ran so long is answered by circumstance rather than by temperament. Barnes points to the parting — "the fact that Paul was about to leave them on the next day, probably to see them no more, was the principal reason" — and cautions that "we are not to suppose... that it was one continued or set discourse. No small part of the time might have been passed in hearing and answering questions." Calvin admires both parties, since "it was no trouble to Paul to teach until midnight, though he were ready to take his journey"; Wesley puts it down to "uncommon fervour of spirit".

The lamps are read as an answer to a slander. Barnes says the detail "meets one of the slanders of the early enemies of Christianity, that Christians in their assemblies were accustomed to extinguish all the lights, and to commit every kind of abomination"; Wesley, that they were there "to prevent any possible scandal"; Gill enters a caution of his own, that this "no ways countenances the use of lamps and wax candles in the daytime at divine worship, since this was in the night".

Ellicott makes the room an argument. It was on the third floor, and "in the high narrow streets of Eastern towns the upper storey is often chosen for social or devotional purposes"; such a room "might well hold two or three hundred people"; and "the vividness and minuteness of the account indicate that we have the narrative of an eye-witness". He and Clarke agree the lamps explain the sleep, Clarke reporting Quesnel's view that the smoke was the cause and that Paul mentions it "in charity, to excuse the young man's appearing negligent".

Calvin will not have the sleeper blamed. "I see no cause why some interpreters should so sore and sharply condemn the drowsiness of the young man, that they should say that he was punished for his sluggishness by death." To seek a comfortable place to sleep "had been a sign of sluggishness, but to be overcome with sleep, sitting at a window, what other thing is it but without fault to yield to nature?" Barnes concedes the point more briefly: "this is an instance of sleeping in public worship that has some apology."

Robertson notes the Greek for window is a diminutive, "a little door", latticed and unglazed, opened "because of the heat from the lamps and the crowd", Ahaziah's fall "through a lattice in his upper chamber" being the nearest parallel; Eutychus, "a common slave name", sat on the sill.
10:
Every voice reaches for the prophets. Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson all read the stretching and the embrace against Elijah at 1 Kings 17:21 and Elisha at 2 Kings 4:34; Wesley notes the sharper point, that "our Lord never used this gesture. But Elijah and Elisha did as well as Paul." Clarke qualifies the parallel: the lying-on "might not have been continued so long" here, "nor indeed was it necessary, as the natural warmth had not yet left the body of Eutychus; but the son of the Shunammite had been some time dead."

Calvin denies that imitation is the point at all. The apostles used "certain external rites, whereby they might give the glory to God, the author", and Paul stretches himself out "to no other end, save only that he might more easily stir up himself unto prayer" — perinde agit, acsi se misceret cum mortuo, he acts as if mixing himself up with the young man. "Peradventure, this was done for the imitation of Elisha... Yet the vehemency of his affection did more move him than the emulation of the prophet." He infers from the text that Paul "did not depart from embracing it until he knew that the life was restored again", and that the apostle's chief care was "lest that sorrowful event should shake the faith of the godly".

Whether Eutychus died is openly contested. Barnes takes the plain miracle: "this has all the appearance of having been a miracle. Life was restored to him as Paul spoke." Robertson lays out the other case honestly — Ramsay, Wendt and Zoeckler rest on "his life is in him" to argue a swoon, and Furneaux adds that the friends did not bring him back until morning — then declines to adjudicate: Paul's language "suits that view, but it suits equally well the idea that he had just been restored to life and so is indecisive... One will believe here as the facts appeal to him." At the close he lets Knowling press back, that "living" is pointless unless the boy had been dead. Ellicott simply paints the scene as an eye-witness would, the rush down the staircase with lamps and torches, "the undisturbed calmness of the Apostle", the body left "in the cool night air" while the discourse resumed. Gill allows that Paul may have seen the fall, been told of it, or had "an intimation of it from the Spirit of God".

The meal divides them again. Barnes reasons that since the breaking is "spoken of Paul only, it is evidently distinguished from the celebration of the Lord's Supper"; Robertson thinks it "probably the Eucharist", interrupted by the accident and only now observed. Ellicott describes the loaf as "probably a long roll" from which each piece was broken off as given, and finds no adequate data to decide between communion and a common repast, though "tasting of the heavenly gift" at Hebrews 6:4 inclines him to the former, and he reckons the whole service at seven or eight hours. Clarke marks the change of verb: this is familiar conversation, "very different from" the solemn discourse of the earlier verses — a distinction Robertson confirms. Wesley notes Paul departed "without taking any rest at all."
13:
Paul's twenty-mile walk to Assos while the ship rounded Cape Lectum is the one detail nobody can explain, and everyone tries. Barnes and Clarke agree only on the plain fact that the sea route was much the longer. Henry reads it as deliberate hardship: Paul "had decreed or determined within himself" to walk whatever the importunity urging "his ease or his credit, or the conveniency of a ship", and the ancients mark the land road as rough enough that it "was enough to kill one to go on foot to Assos" — he took it "that he might call on his friends by the way, and do good among them", hastening to Jerusalem but "endeavouring to make every place he came to the better for him". Wesley agrees he walked for the company of the brethren, "although he had passed the night without sleep, and though Assos was of difficult and dangerous access by land."

Calvin proposes the opposite motive and admits he is guessing: "it is uncertain why Paul did choose rather to go by land... I think that he did then eschew the sea for his health's sake." What he will defend is the courtesy — Paul let his companions sail "that he might ease them of the trouble", so that "we see that they did strive among themselves in courtesy and good turns", and he "was so far from requiring things straitly at their hands" that he remitted duties they were willing to render. Ellicott offers two conjectures — a last word of parting counsel to disciples in Mysia, since Paul believed he would never return; or that "after the exciting scene at Troas, he may have been glad to have even a couple of days of comparative solitude for meditation and prayer" before boarding a ship "with all its motley crew". Robertson, noting the paved Roman road and "a beautiful walk in the spring-time", simply grants that "certainly he was entitled to a little time alone."

The itinerary invites the commentators' learning, and Ellicott alone rebukes it. Chios, Samos and Trogyllium each carry classical associations, "but these, we may well believe... were nothing to the Apostle and his companions" — not the revolt of Mitylene, not Polycrates, not "the blind old man of Scio's rocky isle." He adds the one fact that matters, that Miletus "was practically the port of Ephesus, the harbour of which had been gradually choked by the accumulation of silted-up sand." Robertson tracks Luke's three different phrases for successive days and rejects the Received Text's addition of Trogyllium as "clearly not genuine". Clarke and Barnes fill in the geography and the wines.

On the bypassing of Ephesus, Barnes and Ellicott both stop to say that the English "sail by" is ambiguous: it means to pass it without landing. Gill supplies the motive Paul does not — he feared "he should be detained by the brethren there". Robertson recalls that the riot was only a year old, "not expedient to go back so soon", and that only some thirty days remained. Calvin insists the haste was not reverence for a legal feast — "not that he made so great account of the day", but that strangers gathered at Jerusalem from all quarters, and he would not neglect the opportunity to show "that the kingdom of Christ was enlarged" and "stop the mouths of the wicked". Ellicott adds a practical reason for summoning the elders rather than going: at Miletus "it was in his power to embark at any moment."
17:
Henry sees the whole arrangement as a man managing his own escape. The ship "attended him on purpose, and staid or moved as he pleased"; Paul summoned the elders to Miletus rather than going up "for if he had gone up to Ephesus, he could never have got away from them." He guesses the elders included the twelve who received the Holy Ghost by Paul's hands, plus others Timothy had ordained, and notes that the address is designed to travel: "what instructions he gave to them they would give to the people under their charge." Gill puts the distance at four hundred furlongs or ten German miles, Barnes at forty; Robertson at "some thirty miles, a stiff day's journey each way", so the elders reached him on the third day of his stay.

That these elders are the bishops of v.28 is agreed, and the agreement is unusually flat. Clarke traces the word down: from presbyteros come the Latin, French and English forms and "our own term priest; and all, when traced up to their original, signify merely an elderly or aged person." He thinks the eldership "was not so properly constituted, but which rose out of the state of things", the overseers being selected from among those eldest "in years, Christian knowledge, and experience". Ellicott calls the two names "interchangeable at this period",, each presbyter probably representing "a distinct church or congregation". Robertson makes the same identification from Titus 1:5 and holds that the bishop-over-elders office had not yet developed in the first century. Wesley reduces it to a parish: elders and bishops were "no otherwise different than are the rector of a parish and his curates."

Chrysostom alone asks why Paul speaks of himself at all, and answers that he does it as unwillingly as possible. "Finding himself under a necessity of saying certain great things about himself, he tries to make the least he can of it", and so "first he adduces their own testimony" rather than his own claim. The pattern is scriptural: Samuel delivering up the government asks "have I taken aught of your hands?" (1 Samuel 12:3); David disbelieved recounts the bear (1 Samuel 17:34); Paul tells the Corinthians "I am become a fool; ye have compelled me" (2 Corinthians 12:11). "Nay, God Himself also does the same, not speaking of himself upon any and every occasion, but only when He is disbelieved, then He brings up His benefits."

Calvin reaches the same defence by another road. The sermon's whole burden is to exhort the pastors "by his own example, to do their duty faithfully. For that is the true kind of censure... when the teacher prescribeth nothing which he himself hath not done indeed before." Ambition is "nothing less tolerable in the servants of Christ", but Paul's modesty was known well enough that no suspicion could attach; he extols his labours "not that he may purchase commendation at the hands of his auditory, but that his holy exhortation may pierce more deeply, and may stick fast in their minds" — "and he citeth eye-witnesses, lest he seem to speak of things unknown."

Ellicott rests the discourse's authenticity on that very quality: Luke was present and could take notes, and "no writer of a history adorned with fictitious speeches could have written a discourse so essentially Pauline in all its turns and touches of thought". Barnes finds it "one of the most tender, affectionate, and eloquent" passages anywhere, and Wesley the shortest word of all: "happy is he who can thus appeal to the conscience of his hearers." Robertson dates the arrival to the spring of 51 or 52, making the actual ministry about two and a half years — "roughly three years"; Clarke reports the Bezan addition "for three years, and even more" and judges the time "too long."
19:
"Serving the Lord" is read two ways. Barnes takes it broadly — "to discharge aright our duties in any vocation is serving the Lord" — and draws a moral: eminent success "tends to produce lowliness and humbleness of mind." Clarke likewise extends it past the apostolic office "to his private walk as a Christian". Calvin narrows it deliberately: here it means "not for to worship God in holiness and righteousness, which is common to all the godly; but it doth signify to execute a public function." Paul speaks "not as some one private man, but as one made a minister of the Church."

Gill spells out what the humility cost — no "claiming a dominion over the faith of men", and the refusal even of "what he had a just right unto, a maintenance from the people". Calvin adds the sharper reading: Paul is reckoning up not merely straits but contempt, since "he was not honorably received or with commendation; but he was conversant among them under the contemptible form of the cross", and it is "no small trial... when we faint not, though we see ourselves trodden under foot by the intolerable pride of the world." Ellicott makes the tears a deliberate repudiation of philosophy: Paul's sensitivity "had not been hardened into a Stoic apathy, and therefore found vent in a form which the Stoic would have scorned as unmanly" — where the Stoic manual barely permits outward mourning and warns, "take heed that thou mourn not inwardly." He notes too that the lying in wait of the Jews is distinct from the Demetrian tumult and "implies unrecorded sufferings". Wesley collects the parallel passages and concludes that "holy tears, from those who seldom weep on account of natural occurrences, are no mean specimen of the efficacy and proof of the truth of Christianity" — and that they are consistent with joy, since "the same person may be sorrowful, yet always rejoicing."

On "kept back nothing" the nautical metaphor is contested at the level of confidence rather than substance. Ellicott says the verb "belongs to the vocabulary of sailors, and was used for taking in or reefing sails": Paul had gone on "as it were, before the wind, with all his canvas spread." Robertson allows the sea metaphor as apt for a man so recently aboard ship, but holds the ordinary middle sense sufficient — "to withdraw oneself, to cower, to shrink, to conceal, to dissemble". Ellicott alone registers a limit: even here Paul confines the claim to what was profitable, and what was profitable was measured by capacity, Ephesus proving wider than Corinth.

Barnes turns it into a rule of office: the minister must judge what profits, his aim being neither "to please their fancy" nor "to flatter their pride", and the unpalatable doctrine "should be, and will be delivered". Clarke quotes an old figure of the good shepherd who keeps "abundance of bread in his scrip, and his dog under command" — the dog being zeal, to be moderated; the bread, useful knowledge. Wesley presses the public-and-private pairing hard: without both "he had not been pure from their blood. For even an apostle could not discharge his duty by public preaching only. How much less can an ordinary pastor!"Calvin reduces the whole to three heads — thorough teaching, house-by-house particularity, a summary doctrine — and insists Scripture "doth not contain profound speculations to delight men", so that whoever turns aside to frivolous questions "shall do nothing else but walk in a circuit."

Repentance and faith are the sum, and Clarke guards the order: humiliation "is no atonement for sin; therefore repentance is insufficient, unless faith in our Lord Jesus Christ accompany it." Ellicott observes that from these two "might be developed a whole system of theology"; Wesley finds the movement earlier still — "the very first motion of the soul toward God is a kind of repentance."
22:
"Bound in the spirit" splits the company, and the split is over whose spirit. Clarke and Barnes take it of the Holy Ghost. Barnes calls the phrase "one of great strength and emphasis"; Clarke puts the sense in Paul's own mouth — "I have now no choice — God has not left me either to the advices of friends, or to my own prudence: the Spirit of God obliges me to go to Jerusalem." Gill canvasses and rejects three lesser readings — inward distress, obligation to carry the collection, settled resolve — before landing on the Spirit.

Ellicott decides the other way, "on the whole" for the higher element of Paul's own nature, reserving that the word "points to that part of his being which was most in communion with the Divine Spirit" — a constraint "which virtually limited the freedom of his human will". Robertson agrees, and gives the textual reason: the explicit "Holy Spirit" of the next verse "seems to be in contrast to his own spirit here." He concedes the distance is small, "his own spirit" being "under the control of the Holy Spirit".

How the warnings reached him divides them again. Barnes leans toward direct influence deepened by experience: stoned and scourged in nearly every city, Paul "regarded it as his certain portion to be thus afflicted." Ellicott insists it "can hardly refer to mere internal previsions" but implies prophetic utterance in city after city, of which "we have no separate record"; Calvin says the same — "I do not understand this of secret oracles, but of those foretellings which he heard everywhere of the prophets" — and says why Paul credits the Spirit rather than the speakers: "the word of God hath his authority, when we confess that the Spirit of God is the author thereof, though the ministers be men." Wesley concurs that the revelation came "not immediately, but by the ministry of others."

Cyril of Jerusalem puts the verse to a use none of the others contemplate, gathering it with Philip and the chariot and with the call of Barnabas and Saul, as evidence that the Spirit speaks and acts as a person: "beholdest thou the Spirit living, separating, calling, and with authority sending forth?"

Calvin turns the foreknowledge against excuse-making. Since the Spirit that foretells the bonds "doth also hold him fast bound that he cannot refuse to submit himself unto him", it follows that "what dangers soever hang over our heads, we are not thereby acquitted"; "in vain do those men flatter themselves, who will do good so long as they be free from molestation." He also explains why Paul both knows and does not know: he "speaketh doubtfully at the first of set purpose, that he may soften that which was about to be more bitter".

On the refusal of self-regard, Clarke reads ownership: "I am not my own; my life and being are the Lord's... I act under his direction, and am not anxious about the issue." Barnes generalises: "duty is of more importance than life; and when either duty or life is to be sacrificed, life is to be cheerfully surrendered." Calvin guards the gift itself — life is "ordained to be unto us as a race", yet "it is a filthy thing for us to be so holden with a blind desire to live, that we lose the causes of life for life itself." Ellicott and Robertson both note the racecourse image reaching to Paul's last letter, and Ellicott argues that "with joy" is absent from the best manuscripts, "probably inserted as a rhetorical improvement" — "the passage is grander without them." Wesley adds the observation that gives the whole its weight: such contempt of the world was uttered not by men "who talked elegantly of despising the world in the full affluence of all its enjoyments; but by men who daily underwent the greatest calamities."
25:
"Ye all shall see my face no more" is the hardest sentence in the chapter, because the Pastoral Epistles seem to falsify it, and everyone here knows it. Barnes reads expectation rather than prophecy — Paul had "no expectation of being again at Ephesus", given the danger and his designs on Rome — then concedes, "it is probable, however, that he did again return to that city." Clarke offers two escapes — the words may bind only those present, or only Ephesus and Miletus — then declines both, since Paul writes elsewhere "with a measure of uncertainty... The Holy Spirit did not think proper to give him a direct revelation on this point."

Ellicott states it sharply — if the Pastorals are genuine, Paul revisited Asia, Troas, Miletus and probably Ephesus — and answers twice. First on principle: "the Apostle expressly disclaims foresight of his own future", and "I know" is said "after the manner of men who take the fulfilment of their purpose for granted." Then in a lower key: when he did return, "and all were turned away from him... how many of that company was he likely to have met again?" Robertson concurs: "there need be no surprise that Paul's fears turned out otherwise. He had reason enough for them."

Calvin asks not whether it was true but why it was said. Paul "did put them out of hope of his return, to the end he might more deeply imprint in their minds his exhortations. For we know what great force the words and speeches of men have which are uttered at their departure or death." A second motive follows: they must not "depend upon his presence, and so their faith should faint through wearisomeness." Wesley says it in one line: "he wisely inserts this, that what follows might make the deeper impression." Calvin adds that the kingdom of God here means the gospel doctrine, which begins that kingdom "in this world, by renewing men after the image of God."

Ellicott traces the purity from blood to the watchman of Ezekiel 3:18: Paul "had acted on the teaching of that prophet, and none could require the blood of any man at his hands." Barnes limits what is claimed — "this does not mean that he set up a claim to absolute perfection", only "a conscience void of offence" in this matter — and extends the appeal to any faithful minister, who at the judgment "may call on them to witness that the fault of the ruin of the soul is not to be charged to them." Robertson is guarded: "it is much for any preacher to claim and it ought to be true of all." Clarke states the converse — whoever perishes "shall be accessary to his own perdition" — and Wesley the contrapositive: otherwise "their blood would have been on his head." Calvin notes the appeal is made "not so much for his own cause, as that he may prescribe unto them their duty with greater authority", and rules that pastors must "not esteem at their pleasure what is profitable to be uttered and what to be omitted."

On "all the counsel of God" Gill draws the boundary: not "the purposes and decrees of God, latent in his own breast" — those Paul could not declare — "but his revealed will in the Gospel". Barnes names two ways a truth is suppressed without being denied: avoiding it "from timidity, or an apprehension of giving offence", or "giving it too little prominency". Clarke hears an echo of the Septuagint at Isaiah 9:6, where the wonderful counsellor becomes "the messenger of the great counsel" — a version "constantly under his eye" — so that to declare the counsel is to declare Christ. Ellicott finds a compliment in the phrase: it points "to a greater degree of receptivity for Divine truth than had been found elsewhere."
28:
The order — themselves first, then the flock — is pressed hardest by Calvin. "That man will never be careful for the salvation of other men who will neglect his own", and "will not take pains with his flock who forgetteth himself, seeing he is a part of the flock." He gives four reasons for vigilance: they are bound to the flock; the Holy Ghost and not mortal man called them; governing the Church is "no small honor"; and God has shown "what account he doth make of the Church, seeing that he hath redeemed it with his blood." Pastors "are not free after they be made pastors, but they be bound publicly to all the flock." Barnes lists the hazards implied — "flattery, and ambition, and despondency, and worldly-mindedness" — and adds that without heed "all his preaching will be vain." Gill names the objects of heed: gifts, time, temper, conversation, doctrine.

On the appointment Wesley is absolute: "no man, or number of men upon earth, can constitute an overseer, bishop, or any other Christian minister. To do this is the peculiar work of the Holy Ghost." Ellicott unpacks the appointing into the inward call, its attestation by prophecy, and the bestowal of gifts, and prefers "set you as watchers", since overseer here runs with the shepherd imagery rather than later church order. Clarke will not let the office go cheap: it is "of most awful responsibility; few there are who can fill it", and fewer still "who discharge the duties of it."

"The church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood" is the chapter's live textual dispute. Robertson is flat: the reading is "the church of God", "not 'the church of the Lord'", so "Jesus is here called 'God' who shed his own blood for the flock." He forestalls the objection that Paul never calls Jesus God by citing passages where he does. Clarke, weighing the manuscripts, comes down the other way — "the greater evidence appears to be in favor of tou Kuriou, feed the Church of the Lord" — then refuses the concession any doctrinal damage: "we must maintain that, had not this Lord been God, his blood could have been no purchase for the souls of a lost world."

Ellicott, accepting the received text, sees the argument cut both ways: Paul's habitual "church of God" is evidence for it, and equally the reason a scribe might "substitute a familiar for an unfamiliar phrase." He then infers that the words sanction predicating of the divine nature what belongs to the human — the ancient "passion of my God", the title Theotokos — while judging the New Testament's drift to run the other way, which "tends at once to greater accuracy of thought." Henry has no hesitation: "the blood was his as Man; yet so close is the union between the Divine and human nature, that it is there called the blood of God, for it was the blood of Him who is God." Wesley draws the pastoral conclusion instead: "how precious is it then in his sight!"

The wolves divide them mildly. Clarke takes "after my departing" of "his death; for few of these evils took place during his life"; Robertson denies it — "not his death, but his departure from them" — and canvasses Judaizers and a coming Gnostic shadow without deciding. Barnes and Wesley look outward, Barnes to Jews approaching "with great professed friendship". Ellicott holds the wolf stands "primarily for the open enemies of the flock, the persecutors of all ages", while allowing wolves in sheep's clothing — the next verse's subject. Calvin turns it into weather: God grants fair seasons in which "the sheep are fed more safely in the fields", but "there is more danger when the air is cloudy and dark", a season "more fit for the subtilty of wolves". No time to sleep.
30:
The second danger is the worse one, and everyone says so. Barnes states it flatly: "the church of Christ would have little to fear from external enemies if it nurtured no foes in its own bosom." He names the type — men moved by ambition or "the love of power or popularity" — and instances Diotrephes, Phygellus, Hymenæus and Alexander; Gill produces much the same roll. Ellicott adds the detail that gives the scene its ache: the later epistles show how exactly Paul foresaw this, and "it adds to the pathos of this parting to think that men such as Hymenæus and Philetus may have been actually present, listening to the Apostle's warnings, and warned by him in vain." Robertson widens the catalogue to false philosophy, immorality and asceticism, Paul's long residence having "enabled him to judge clearly of conditions there".

On the motive the commentators converge on ambition and diverge on how the damage is done. Calvin makes it an axiom: "ambition is the mother of all heresies." The word flourishes "when the pastors join hand in hand to bring disciples unto Christ, because this alone is the sound state of the Church, that he be heard alone." He grades the offenders too: those who merely fail their duty are hirelings, "not so hurtful as the other", whereas "the corruption of doctrine is a most deadly plague to the sheep." Ellicott sharpens the phrase to "draw away the disciples", those already Christ's, and finds the note of heresy in its self-assertion. Robertson observes drily that "such leaders of dissension can always gain a certain following",.

Clarke alone works out a causal sequence, and it begins with the pastors, not the schismatics. Superintendents "lose the life of God, neglect the souls of the people, become greedy of gain"; the neglected members "get their minds alienated from their rapacious pastors"; and only then do "men of sinister views take advantage of this state of distraction, foment discord, preach up the necessity of division".

"Watch" is heard as an echo. Ellicott traces it to the Lord's own teaching, "which could hardly have been unknown to St. Paul", and gives it a fresh edge from the office: "they who were the bishops, the overseers, the watchers of the flock, ought, above all others, to set an example of vigilance." Robertson notes the imperative is the very form of Christ's command about the perils before his return — "stay awake" — and glosses Paul's admonishing verb "to put sense into one". Clarke names the two failures the command guards against: "unwatchfulness and forgetfulness are two grand inlets to apostasy."

The three years are handled by arithmetic. Barnes counts three months in the synagogue and two years in the school of Tyrannus, allows some months more, and offers as alternatives "merely a round number" or the Jewish custom of counting part of a year as a year. Ellicott makes the same sum plus "an undefined period embracing the time immediately before and after the tumult of Demetrius" — enough to warrant "speaking roughly" of three years. Clarke agrees the Greek "does not necessarily mean three whole years", and reports one manuscript so troubled by the shortfall that it substitutes two years. Calvin asks rather who was admonished: the "every one" may cover the whole church, since Paul "speaketh as if the whole body were present", or be restrained to the pastors. Either way the appeal is again to his own example, and it is "an unseemly thing that they should be wearied who had seen his singular patience by the space of three years". Wesley closes with the sting: "this was watching indeed! Who copies after this example?"
32:
Chrysostom reads the turn to prayer as tact. Paul had "much alarmed them" with the wolves, and so, "not to overpower them, and make them lose all self-possession, observe the consolation": he commends them to the word of his grace — "that is, to His grace: it is grace that saveth." Grace is invoked constantly "to make them more earnest as being debtors", and one word is pressed hard: Paul "does not say, to build, but, 'to build up,' showing that they had already been built." Calvin defends the same movement against the rhetoricians: Paul "did not pass for dividing his sermon into parts", since "no words were sufficient to express the vehemency of the affections wherewith he was inflamed", and what follows is "rather an expressing of a desire than a direct prayer". Though addressed to pastors, he holds it "doth also comprehend the whole Church".

What "the word of his grace" can do provokes the tile's finest hesitation. Ellicott concedes that "it can hardly be said that the 'word' here is used, as it is by St. John, for the person of Christ", yet notes "a quasi-personal character ascribed to it... which suggests something more than the written or spoken word." He locates the explanation in the implanted word and the living word of Hebrews, "a preparation for the more fully developed teaching of St. John as to the Logos." Barnes stays with the doctrine, but reaches for the same energetic texts: the word "quick... and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword", "like a hammer that breaketh the rock". Robertson keeps the agency with God, who "works through the word of his grace and so it is able to build up", and observes that build and inheritance among the sanctified recur in the letter to these same Ephesians.

Clarke turns the metaphor into numbered stages — the soul once God's habitation now "in a state of ruin"; Christ the only foundation; God's grace the "model, or plan, according to which the building can be raised". Wesley aims the corollary at the confident: God "can thus build us up, without any instrument. But he does build us up by them. O beware of dreaming that you have less need of human teachers after you know Christ than before!" Gill catches the courtesy: Paul calls the elders brethren and "puts himself upon a level with them".

Nearly everyone hears the disclaimer of covetousness as an echo of Samuel's, several as a reply to slander. Ellicott gives the reason each was needed: Samuel's sons "had been guilty of corrupt practices, taking bribes", while against Paul it was charged that he used his ministry "as a cloke of covetousness". Robertson names the charge — that the collection for the poor was really for himself — and explains the third item: "oriental wealth consisted largely in fine apparel". Barnes argues from opportunity: the early Christians committed their property to the apostles, so "if the object of Paul had been to make money, he might have availed himself, and have become enriched" — which makes the open appeal "one of the incidental but striking proofs of the Christian religion".

Chrysostom fixes on the verb: "he says not, I have not taken, but, not even 'coveted'" — the love of money being "the root of evils". Calvin agrees the denial reaches past extortion to desire itself, and infers: "no man can be a good minister of the word, but he must also contemn money", since "nothing is more common, than that those corrupt the word of God, to win the favor of men, who are altogether filthily given to get gain." Clarke makes it a test: by this mark "they would be able to discover the grievous wolves, and the perverters", who "had nothing but their own interests in view." Gill adds that the vindication is offered less for Paul than "for their imitation".
34:
The tent-making hands defend working ministers, not a rule against paid ones. Clarke says it twice: it was "neither sin nor discredit" for Paul to work, and, many being still so obliged, "whatever it may be to the people, it is no cause of reproach to the minister." Barnes puts the discredit on "a people who put him under a necessity to toil for his support", and makes the verse a test: every minister should live so as to make this appeal "from the pulpit... or when on a dying bed". Wesley cuts to the image: "these hands — callous, as you see, with labour. Who is he that envies such a bishop or archbishop as this?"

Calvin is the one who insists on what the verse does not establish. Paul "doth not, in these words, precisely set down a law which all the ministers of the word must needs keep", nor "so loftily and lordlike" take away "that which the Lord had granted to his servants" — he elsewhere defends the minister's right to maintenance, accepted food and raiment from many churches, and said of his need at Corinth that he robbed other churches to relieve it. The Corinthians had not withheld his due; the refusal answered false apostles who boasted of working for nothing. The example is offered "how far forth he exhorteth them to follow" it, not as a statute.

Whom the hands supported is settled by inference. Ellicott notes Paul "had not been satisfied with working for himself, but ministered also to those who were with him", and reasons from his rule against idleness that these were "suffering from infirmity"; a letter from Ephesus supplies "an undesigned coincidence confirming the statement". Robertson names Aquila and Priscilla and adds Timothy "because of his often infirmities", Paul having "pointed to his hands with pride". Barnes and Ellicott agree the weak are the sick and needy; Robertson widens it: "this noble plea to help the weak is the very spirit of Christ", the toiling being "not just for ourselves, but to help... at the other end."

The unrecorded saying is handled with confidence and care. Barnes points out the evangelists "did not pretend to record all his sayings", many being "treasured up by those who heard them". Ellicott claims more: the words appear in no canonical gospel "nor indeed in any of the Apocryphal", and evidence "the wide diffusion of an oral teaching... of which the four Gospels are but partial representatives"; the command to remember implies they "had often been prominent in the Apostle's teaching". Robertson calls it "one of the sayings of Jesus in current use that Paul had received and treasured", others surviving in ancient writers and new papyri, genuine or not. Clarke rests it on the apostle's word: "that our Lord did speak them, St. Paul's evidence is quite sufficient to prove. The sentiment is worthy of Christ."

Clarke gives the beatitude its most humane reading, turned toward the receiver. "A truly generous mind, in affluence, rejoices in opportunities to do good", but "a man of an independent spirit, when reduced to poverty, finds it a severe trial to be obliged to live on the bounty of another, and feels pain in receiving what the other feels a happiness in communicating." The conclusion is a rule of manners: "let the man who is able to give feel himself the obliged person, and think how much pain the feeling heart of his supplicant must endure." Wesley reads it theologically — to give is "to imitate God, and have him, as it were, indebted to us" — and limits the labouring sensibly, "so far as the labours of your office allow you time". Barnes and Gill note the appeal is example, not precept: Paul did "not merely discourse about it, but showed you how to do it", setting a pattern "in every point, and particularly in this".
36:
The kneeling draws more comment than the prayer, which is not reported. Ellicott reads the omission generously: the historian who recorded the charge "shrinks, with a natural reverence, from reporting his prayer" — and points to the great intercession in the letter to these same Ephesians for "its substance, perhaps even its very thoughts and words." Barnes and Clarke agree kneeling is "the proper posture of a supplicant", arguing "at once both humility and submission". Robertson concedes more room: "kneeling in prayer is a fitting attitude... though not the only proper one."

Calvin gives the gesture a small theology. Inward affection is "the chiefest thing in prayer", yet the outward signs have a double use: "that we exercise all our members to the glory and worship of God", and "that by this exercise our sluggishness may be awakened". Public prayer adds a third, since by it "the children of God make profession of their godliness".Kneeling testifies humility. Paul seals the sermon with prayer "because we can hope for no profit of our doctrine, save only from the blessing of God", so whoever would "do any good by teaching, admonishing, and exhorting" should "always end after this sort."

Henry fastens on the word with. It was "a joint prayer. He not only prayed for them, but prayed with them, prayed with them all", so they might offer the same petitions and "learn what to ask of God for themselves when he was gone" — public prayers being "designed to quicken and encourage" secret ones, not to supersede them.

The weeping provokes the tile's one quarrel, and it is with the Stoics. Gill states the principle: "Christians are not Stoics, religion does not take away and destroy the natural affections, but regulates and governs them, and directs to a right use of them." Calvin presses it into argument. Since the Spirit "commendeth their tears... as witnesses of sincere godliness, he condemneth the rashness of those who require at the hands of the faithful hard and cruel constancy"; false is the dream "that those affections proceed only of corruption, which we have naturally from God." The conclusion is exact: "the perfection of the faithful consisteth not in this, that they put off all affections; but that they be moved therewith only for just causes." Wesley turns it on his own age: of old "the best and bravest of men were easily melted into tears... But now, notwithstanding the effeminacy which almost universally prevails, we leave those tears to women and children."

What they wept for was not sentiment: "they did bewail their own condition, and the condition of all the whole church of Asia", "deprived of an inestimable treasure." Ellicott sets the parting beside David and Jonathan's, noting "the absence of any suppression of emotion", the elders eager for the last embrace "up to the very hour of embarkation". Barnes and Clarke supply the gesture's ordinariness — the neck, the kiss, Joseph meeting Jacob — while Robertson catches the tense: intensive and imperfect, so "they kept on kissing", probably one after another.

Barnes ends in self-examination: true religion "makes the heart more tender", and ministers should so live as to "look back upon their whole ministry as pure and disinterested", that "so parting, they may part in peace." Clarke finds the pathos in the man — the one "who had first pointed out to them the Lord Jesus Christ" now leaving, "to be seen no more till the day in which the quick and dead shall stand before the throne of judgment" — then uses the chapter's opening to argue that the Lord's day has been set apart "ever since the apostolic times". Wesley takes the darkest turn of the phrase: "what sorrow will be in the great day, when God shall speak that word to all who are found on the left hand, that they shall see his face no more!"
